description:
Castello di Bevilacqua was built in 1336 by Guglielmo Bevilacqua and completed by his son Francesco on behalf of the ruling Scaligeri lordship, conceived as a fortress to defend against the neighboring Carraresi and Este powers. Starting around 1532, Gianfrancesco Bevilacqua commissioned architect Michele Sanmicheli to thoroughly modernize the medieval structure, transforming it into a villa with more comfortable, refined interiors — a transformation continued in 1756 when Gaetano Ippolito Bevilacqua restored much of the castle's interior, and again in 1860 when Felicita Bevilacqua and her husband gave the complex its present Neo-Gothic appearance, in keeping with the Romantic taste of the era.

Since 1990, the Iseppi-Cerato family has led an extensive restoration effort, returning Sanmicheli's 16th-century interiors to their former splendor. Today the castle holds a genuinely dual identity: a working 14-room hotel with just seven "dream scenes" and seven junior suites, and a real day-visit heritage site, open to the public daily for a self-guided tour through the museum route, with guided Sunday tours exploring the castle's 700-year history in greater depth.

Michele Sanmicheli, the architect responsible for the castle's 16th-century transformation, was one of the most significant military and civil architects of Renaissance Venice, and his work at Bevilacqua reflects the broader trend of Veneto noble families modernizing their medieval fortresses into more comfortable residences as the region's defensive needs diminished under Venetian rule.

The castle's three distinct renovation phases — Sanmicheli's 16th-century villa conversion, the 1756 interior restoration, and the 1860 Neo-Gothic remodeling — give Bevilacqua a genuinely layered architectural history, with each period leaving its own mark on the building rather than a single unified restoration erasing earlier work.

The Iseppi-Cerato family's post-1990 restoration, specifically focused on recovering Sanmicheli's original 16th-century interiors, represents a deliberate curatorial choice to prioritize one particular historical layer of the castle's development, giving today's visitors and guests a genuinely Renaissance-era interior experience within the Neo-Gothic exterior shell.

The castle's genuine day-visit museum route, open daily with additional Sunday guided tours, distinguishes Bevilacqua from many castle-hotels in this collection where no independent heritage-visit product exists — visitors here can experience 700 years of documented history regardless of whether they book an overnight stay.

Montagnana, the walled Renaissance town a short drive from Bevilacqua, is one of the best-preserved fortified towns in the Veneto, giving guests staying at the castle an easy pairing between Bevilacqua's own layered architectural history and a genuinely intact medieval-to-Renaissance urban fortification nearby.

faqs.question: Can I visit Bevilacqua Castle without staying overnight?
faqs.answer: Yes — the castle is open to the public daily 9:30-18:30 for a self-guided museum route (about 30 minutes, €5 for adults), with guided tours available on Sundays 10:30-11:30 (€10 for adults) covering the castle's 700-year history.

faqs.question: Who was Michele Sanmicheli and why does he matter at Bevilacqua Castle?
faqs.answer: Sanmicheli was a leading Renaissance military and civil architect who, starting in 1532, transformed the medieval fortress into a more comfortable villa. His 16th-century interiors were specifically restored by the current owners after 1990.

faqs.question: How many rooms does the hotel at Bevilacqua Castle have?
faqs.answer: Just 14 in total — seven "dream scenes" and seven junior suites — all within the historic castle building itself.

hotel.how_to_stay:
**Getting there:** About 15 minutes by car from Montagnana's walled old town; roughly 45 minutes from Verona and 1h from Padua.

**Rooms & rates:** Just 14 rooms total (7 "dream scenes" plus 7 junior suites), all within the historic castle building itself. From €149/night.

**On-site:** Restaurant, on-site museum route (self-guided daily, guided Sundays), gardens, 16 event halls with period furnishings.

**Good to know:** This is a genuinely small property — only 14 rooms — so it books up quickly, especially around weddings and events; the castle's museum route is open to day visitors independent of a hotel stay.

**Combine with:** The walled Renaissance town of Montagnana, a short drive away.
